subject: hedgehog
pitch: A plump hedgehog out on an autumn evening walk. A dome of spines in chestnut brown with cream tips, a soft fawn face with a pointed, twitchy snout, a shiny black button nose, tiny round ears and bright beady eyes. Little pink paws, and a single red maple leaf stuck on its spines like a trophy.
reasoning:
I'm planning a realistic hedgehog model for the 3js builder SDK, working out proportions based on real-world dimensions—around 24cm body length with a plump, rounded body shape.

I'm sketching the skeleton structure with a spine chain from rump to head, then designing the body as a sweep along a curved path with varying radius to create a fat midsection. For the spines themselves, I'm figuring out how to use the spike tool with chestnut brown coloring and cream tips, likely scattered across the body's dome surface.

Now I'm worried about part budget: if each spike with bands creates two mesh pieces, scattering hundreds of spines across the dome could blow past the 1000-part limit, so I'm reconsidering a merged-geometry approach instead — building individual cone shapes in three.js, positioning and orienting them using the surface scatter and normal data, then merging them into one mesh per color to keep the part count low while still achieving the spiny look.

Checking whether a skinned joint produces one mesh per color piece, since spikes sit on blended-weight areas of the body and should still resolve to a single mesh. I'm weighing an alternative using `b.stick` with cone geometry per spine, potentially using a paint function to vary color along the cone's UV coordinates instead of creating separate parts for the tip color — tracing through how cone/cylinder UV.v maps to height to get the color gradient right.

Now I'm working out the cone's orientation and how `embed` positions it relative to its own height along the stick's facing axis.

The docs example confirms a centered geometry with embed 0.5 sits with its center exactly at the surface, half in and half out. For a spine I want more tip exposed than base sunk, so I'm considering translating the cone so its base sits at the geometry origin, then using a small embed value like 0.2 to sink just the base region while most of the tip projects outward.

Rather than fuss over exact embed semantics, I realize b.spike is purpose-built for this — it builds a cone from a base frame toward a tip point with configurable radius and cap style. I'm weighing cap options (round, flat, point, none) for the base and tip, since a round cap at the zero-radius tip looks fine, and the base cap style matters for how cleanly it sits against the surface.

With roughly 200 spines each producing 1-2 mesh parts via sweep, I'm estimating around 400 total parts, which seems manageable. I also need to account for spine direction tilting backward rather than purely following the surface normal, so I'm thinking about blending the normal vector with a backward lean to get a more natural hedgehog-spine look.

For scattering spines over the body surface, I'll use the scatter function with a minimum distance and a filter so spines only appear on the back and sides, excluding the face, belly, and leg regions — filtering based on each hit's normal direction and position along the body.

Now I'm sizing the hedgehog's proportions: body radius around 6cm, spine length about 3.5cm, with the body axis positioned so the belly clears the floor and legs are short stubs reaching down to the paws.

I'm placing the legs from hip joints down to visible pink paws, with the pointed snout extending forward from the head so the nose tip juts past the body. Now I'm setting up the actual coordinates and skeleton structure—defining the rump, spine curve, and the joint chain from hips through the spine toward the head.

Thinking through the chain setup, I realize I need to split the spine into a proper joint sequence ending in a neck and head, then use a sweep bone made of these chained joints to shape the body's silhouette with a radius profile.

Writing skeleton joint code...

Still working out the spine chain structure...

Now I'm planning the body shape using a loft along station points from rump to neck base, specifying width and height at each z position to create a plump oval cross-section. I'm checking the vertical math so the body's bottom sits near the floor and the top stays proportional for a stylized hedgehog rather than too tall.

I want the loft bound to the spine bone chain, and I'm thinking through coloring: the body base should be a cream/fawn belly tone, with chestnut spines layered over the dorsal side to create countershading.

For the head, I'm considering a tapered snout — either a separate sweep or a short neck chain extending from the spine's end joint, with a head joint aimed slightly forward and down to shape the pointed nose.

Now I'm working out the spine joint positions along the hip-to-chest path, deciding whether the chain's first joint should duplicate the hips position or whether hips itself should serve as the implicit root of the chain to keep exactly one root joint overall.

I'm deciding to keep the hips joint as the explicit root at the base position, then build the spine chain parented to it with waist and chest joints, accepting a slight positional overlap as harmless. For the neck and head, I'm placing the head joint as a child of chest at an upper position, continuing to work out its aim direction.

Now I'm defining the head shape as a loft through several stations from skull back to a pointed snout tip, each with width/height values that taper down for a twitchy nose effect, and weighing whether to use a loft (elliptical cross-section) versus a sweep (circular) bound to the head joint.

For spines, I'm planning to scatter them only on the body mesh excluding the fawn-colored head region, so the face stays smooth while the back and head-top area get spiny coverage. For the ears, I'm considering a flattened sphere scaled down in one axis to create small round fawn-colored discs attached to the head joint.

I need to double check the local coordinate convention—since the model's left side corresponds to +X locally but world −X, I have to be careful when mirroring ear placement across left and right using the sign loop so they end up symmetric rather than swapped.

I realize that when using explicit literal points for `at`, those coordinates are always in model space regardless of which bone is specified, so I can avoid frame-local confusion entirely by just using model coordinates everywhere. For the eyes, I'll build them as a small black glossy sphere with a tiny white highlight sphere to get that "bright beady eye" look.

For the nose, I'll place a small near-black sphere at the snout tip to serve as the shiny button nose, skipping an actual highlight since the material roughness is fixed. For the paws, I'm planning limb chains from shoulder/hip joints down to the feet, keeping the legs themselves a fawn/dark tone while making just the foot segments pink to match "little pink paws."

Now I'm working out the geometry for the front legs specifically — placing the shoulder root and foot target points, calculating the distance between them, and choosing segment lengths and elbow bend direction so the stubby hedgehog limb looks right, then setting up the chain naming convention (hip/knee/ankle style) so the limb builder knows where to place the tip joint.

For the paw itself, I'm deciding to attach a flattened sphere shape to the chain's tip bone, scaling it unevenly to look more like a little rounded paw rather than a plain ball.

I'm now working out the leg geometry for the hind legs: setting root hip positions and target foot positions, then computing the distances between them to figure out appropriate segment lengths for the bends.

For coloring, I'm making the legs a fawn tone and the paws a soft pink. I'll skip the tail since it's negligible for hedgehogs, and I'm thinking about adding a small maple leaf stuck in the spines as a decorative touch, which will need a lobed polygon outline for extrusion.

Plotting coordinates for a five-lobed leaf shape...

Then I'm assembling the full outline as an ordered list of points: starting at the stem base, moving up through alternating valley and sharp tip points on the right side (D0→D→CD→C→BC→B→AB→A at the top), then mirroring the same sequence down the left side back to the base, and checking that this ordering won't cause the polygon edges to cross.

I decide to mark the lobe tips as sharp corners while leaving the valleys unsharp, so that applying smoothing will round the inner notches while keeping the pointed tips crisp -- this should give a natural maple-leaf silhouette, and the edge lengths are long enough that the smoothing cuts shouldn't overlap or cross adjacent edges.

I settle on a tilted frame where the leaf leans backward about 30 degrees from vertical with its face oriented up-and-forward, so it reads clearly as a leaf stuck trophy-style atop the hedgehog when viewed from the front.

For the spines, I plan to scatter hundreds of small spike shapes across the body surface, filtering out the face, belly, and neck regions, and using a shared paint texture (cream tips fading to chestnut) so all spines render as a single material rather than hundreds of separate parts.
